clinicalPearls: Classic syndrome: bilateral cranial nerve palsies followed by symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis, in a patient who is afebrile and fully conscious with normal sensorium (Harrison 22e p.1235).

First neurologic manifestation is usually ptosis, which can be striking; ocular findings include blurred/fuzzy vision or diplopia from extraocular palsies of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI (Harrison 22e p.1235).

Bulbar onset: dysarthria, difficulty swallowing, and nasal/oral regurgitation reflect cranial nerve involvement; descending weakness then spreads to neck, shoulders, and limbs, with proximal groups affected before distal (Harrison 22e p.1235).
Paralysis descends symmetrically and distal tendon reflexes diminish symmetrically; constipation from intestinal paralysis develops in almost all patients (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236).

In a U.S. series of 332 cases, the most common reported symptoms were difficulty swallowing (86%), fatigue (85%), blurred vision (80%), and slurred speech (78%); signs included afebrile temperature (99%), descending paralysis (93%), alert/oriented status (93%), and ptosis (81%) (Harrison 22e p.1236).

BoNTs irreversibly block acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, so paralysis persists for weeks to months until nerve endings regenerate; the clinical approach is the same for all toxin types causing human illness (Harrison 22e p.1234, p.1236).

Four naturally occurring forms (foodborne, infant, wound, adult intestinal colonization) plus iatrogenic and inhalational forms; the neurologic syndrome is essentially identical across all forms and all ages (Harrison 22e p.1233-1235).

Every case of foodborne botulism is a public health emergency, as it may be the first in an outbreak; clinicians should contact the state health department emergency line to reach a CDC botulism consultant (Harrison 22e p.1235, p.1237).
More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the U.S. recover, and the infant botulism survival rate is near 100% (Harrison 22e p.1236).
harrison.pathophysiology: Disease is caused by botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs) produced by Clostridium botulinum (rarely C. butyricum or C. baratii), gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacteria whose heat-resistant spores are ubiquitous in soil. Serotypes A, B, E, and F cause human disease. BoNT is a metalloprotease whose heavy chain mediates neurospecific binding and internalization and whose light chain enters the cytosol and cleaves SNARE-family proteins (e.g., SNAP-25, VAMP), disrupting synaptic vesicle fusion and blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles. Toxin binding is effectively irreversible, so recovery requires regeneration of nerve endings over weeks to months. Routes differ by form: foodborne (ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly preserved foods, often home-canned low-acid vegetables), wound (spore germination in wounds/necrotic tissue, notably from black tar heroin injection), infant and adult intestinal colonization (in situ toxin production by colonizing Clostridium), iatrogenic (high-dose therapeutic BoNT injection), and inhalational (aerosolized toxin as a bioweapon). (Harrison 22e p.1233-1234)
additionalDifferentials: Basilar stroke producing nonlateralizing/symmetric bulbar palsies
infectionMimics: Guillain-Barre syndrome following Campylobacter jejuni or viral infection
nonInfectiousMimics: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (proximal limb weakness, often with advanced cancer)
Intoxication from alcohol or other substances (ptosis, dysarthria, and gait instability can be misattributed)
additionalInvestigations: Detailed neurologic examination (the key to clinical diagnosis, uncovering invariable cranial nerve deficits)
Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis (protein usually normal in botulism, in contrast to GBS; may help distinguish)
Electromyography by an experienced operator (neuromuscular junction blockage with normal axonal conduction and potentiation on rapid repetitive stimulation)
Brain imaging (normal in botulism; helps exclude basilar stroke)
Serologic antibody tests and rapid nerve stimulation tests (to evaluate myasthenia gravis)
Mouse bioassay (gold standard for BoNT identification and serotyping in clinical or food specimens)
Detection of BoNT in serum or stool, or isolation of BoNT-producing Clostridium from stool or wound cultures; toxin in suspected food
In vitro assays: real-time PCR for bont genes, Endopep mass spectrometry, immune-based and cell-based assays
redFlags: Pharyngeal muscle flaccidity causing airway collapse and respiratory arrest early in the course
Falling vital capacity / diaphragmatic and accessory muscle weakness signaling impending respiratory failure
Rapidly progressive descending paralysis (especially BoNT type A or F)
A placid, expressionless appearance masking the agitation expected with respiratory distress
Two or more patients with the same syndrome (near-pathognomonic and signals an outbreak / public health emergency)
harrison.prognosis: More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the United States recover, often after protracted intensive care and rehabilitation, even without antitoxin; the survival rate for infant botulism is near 100%. Paralysis lasts weeks to months while affected nerve endings regenerate. Serotype A is associated with more rapid progression, more frequent respiratory compromise and mechanical ventilation, and longer-duration paralysis; type B is milder and shorter; type F progresses rapidly but recovers faster. Untreated, early death results from airway obstruction and inadequate tidal volume from respiratory muscle paralysis. (Harrison 22e p.1236)
pitfalls: Misclassifying the paralysis as ascending: botulism is a DESCENDING (cranial-first, then downward) symmetric flaccid paralysis, whereas GBS presents as an ASCENDING paralysis in about 95% of cases - this descending-versus-ascending distinction is central, though the Miller Fisher GBS variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) may resemble early descending paralysis (Harrison 22e p.1236).

Mistaking intact sensorium for altered consciousness: cranial nerve palsies, ptosis, dysarthria, and gait instability can give a false impression of obtundation or be wrongly attributed to alcohol/substance intoxication, even though patients remain fully conscious (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236).

Sporadic (lone) cases are commonly misdiagnosed because of the rarity of botulism and clinician unfamiliarity; an incomplete neurologic examination is a frequent cause of delayed or missed diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1236).
Waiting for laboratory confirmation: confirmation may take >=24 h, so treatment must rely on rapid clinical diagnosis rather than awaiting lab results (Harrison 22e p.1236-1237).

Assuming normal CSF excludes GBS too early: in GBS, CSF protein elevation may lag symptom onset by days, so a normal early CSF must be interpreted with symptom duration and the lumbar puncture may need repeating (Harrison 22e p.1236).

Reported paresthesias are not explained by the known activity of botulinum toxin, and GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting) are seen in foodborne but have NOT been reported in wound botulism (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal numeric severity score; severity is described as varying greatly between patients and is probably governed by toxin dose. At the mild end, some untreated patients progress no further than ptosis and mild palsy of one or two cranial nerves; at the severe end, others develop fulminant cranial nerve palsies and rapidly progressive descending flaccid paralysis affecting most or all voluntary muscles with respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation within hours. (Harrison 22e p.1236)
management: Early administration of equine botulinum antitoxin to neutralise unbound circulating toxin, using human-derived botulism immune globulin for infant botulism
Meticulous supportive intensive care with close monitoring of respiratory function, vital capacity and airway protection
Mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure arising from diaphragmatic and bulbar weakness
For wound botulism, surgical debridement plus penicillin, avoiding aminoglycosides and other agents that potentiate neuromuscular blockade
Nutritional support and management of ileus and constipation from intestinal paralysis
Prolonged rehabilitation over weeks to months while paralysed nerve endings regenerate
Urgent public health notification with investigation and recall of the implicated food source and assessment of exposed contacts
